## INT8-KV DECODE WIRED E2E (2026-08-12 afternoon): +19% 8K decode (144 -> 172 tok/s), the 0.82x gap vs MLX closes to ~0.97x -- opt-in path, one integration bug found + fixed by the e2e gate

WIRING (session_prefill.mojo): per-layer int8 MIRROR buffers ([hk][key][d_head] int8 + per-key f32
scales, +50% KV memory, gated on both blobs) + an INT8 decode table (1 + 8*layers + 2: the f16
split-K table with a re-patchable `_kv_i8_quant_kernel` dispatch after each kvprod and the v4
partial in place of f4u2) + dispatch switch (i8 table takes priority at depth when built) +
budget-count arm. MIRROR UPKEEP via watermark: LAZY SWEEP (quantize [0, n_keys) on the first deep
step after any prefill -- prefill tables write f16 only) then APPEND (the single new key per step);
pos_base=0 prefills reset the watermark. DEFAULT WORKER UNCHANGED: without the two blobs linked,
decode_i8kv_built is False and every path stays byte-identical f16 -- int8 KV is build-time OPT-IN.
INTEGRATION BUG FOUND BY THE E2E GATE: first e2e run violated greedy determinism -- the v4 kernel
indexed the mirror with stride = RUNTIME n_keys (changes every step) while the quant writer uses
the FIXED capacity stride (n_blocks*key_block_size); the partial read a different garbage row each
step. FIXED (mirror stride = fixed capacity, layout note in the module), blob regenerated; the
standalone v4 driver could not catch this (it never ran the quant writer -- recorded as the gap
class e2e gates exist for). RESULTS (post-fix): greedy determinism green at 1K/4K/8K; interleaved
8K decode (256 out @ 8192 in, 3 rounds each): i8kv **172 [135,172,177]** vs f16 tile2048 **144

## GEMM tournament Gate 0, MECHANISM RESOLVED (2026-08-12): llama.cpp's batch amortization is DISPATCH OVERLAP, not cache residency -- fresh-weight differential refutes residency outright; same-day re-measure holds the gap at 2.7x; the lever reframes from scheduling/cache to MMA micro-efficiency

Gate 0's follow-up entry settled that the ~2.7x real GEMM gap (Algenta ~0.596ms/dispatch GPU-only
marginal vs llama.cpp ~0.207ms under dense batching, same real qkv_proj shape M=256/K=1024/N=4096)
is GPU-side, not CPU-encoding, and left ONE open mechanistic question: WHY does llama.cpp's kernel
get ~2x cheaper per dispatch in a dense batch while Algenta's shows zero amortization? The entry's
own named next tool was an Instruments GPU capture; this entry replaces it with two cheaper, more
direct instruments, and resolves the question.

### Instrument 1 (attempted, refuted as an instrument): per-dispatch GPU timestamps

`mm_operator_harness_timestamped.m` (new, additive sibling of `mm_operator_harness_batched.m`,
same pinned kernel/constants/shape/grid): `MTLCommonCounterSetTimestamp` via `MTLCounterSample
Buffer`, sampling around every dispatch inside the batch. The device (AGXG16X / M4 Max) advertises
the timestamp counter set but REJECTS encoder-level sampling at runtime: `-[AGXG16XFamilyCompute
Context sampleCountersInBuffer:atSampleIndex:withBarrier:]: failed assertion '... not supported on
this device'`. Recorded as an API-limitation finding: per-dispatch GPU timestamps inside a compute
stream are NOT available on this Apple silicon generation, which is exactly why the campaign (and
Gate 0's entry) could never measure them. The file guards the unsupported path and still runs the
uninstrumented same-session sweep.

### Machine-state finding (disclosed first, it governs every number below)

This machine has been up **9 days 4 hours** (no reboot since before the tournament), and its GPU
steady state is dramatically different from the Aug 7 cooled state the ledger's absolute numbers
were taken in:

| quantity | Aug 7 (cooled, up ~4-5 days) | Aug 12 (this entry) | drift |
|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp isolated GPU-only | 0.410 ms | **0.747 ms** (p10 0.745 / p90 0.749, reproducible across process launches) | **+82%** |
| llama.cpp batched GPU marginal | 0.205-0.209 ms | **0.204-0.209 ms** | **unchanged** |
| Algenta isolated GPU-only | 0.561-0.573 ms | **0.561 ms** | unchanged |
| Algenta batched GPU marginal | 0.576-0.615 ms | **0.557 ms** (OLS, 8 sweep points) | unchanged |

`pmset -g therm` shows no thermal/performance warnings recorded; macOS 26.5.2 and Xcode-26.6.0
toolchain unchanged since Aug 7 (mtimes verified). The drift manifests as a per-invocation latency
inflation that DENSE STREAMS HIDE (llama.cpp's batched marginal is bit-for-bit stable while its
isolated cost nearly doubled) -- and it does not touch Algenta's kernel at all. Consequence, stated
as a measurement rule: **cross-day absolute comparisons against Aug 7/8 ledger numbers are invalid
on this machine until it is rebooted or the state normalizes; only same-session ratios are
load-bearing.** Every comparison below is same-session.

### Instrument 2 (decisive): the fresh-weight differential -- cache residency REFUTED

If llama.cpp's batch amortization came from the 8MB f16 weight slice staying cache-resident across
back-to-back dispatches (mechanism B), then rotating or freshening the weight buffers should kill
the amortization. `mm_operator_harness_residency.m` (new, additive) batches N=28 and N=112
dispatches three ways -- V0 "shared" (every dispatch reads the same wBuf, the original recipe),
V1 "rot8" (dispatch d reads weight copy d%8, a 64MB rotating working set), V2 "fresh" (dispatch d
reads weight copy d -- N distinct copies, 224MB at N=28 and **896MB at N=112, far beyond any L2/SLC
capacity, every dispatch guaranteed cache-cold**) -- all copies holding identical data, GPU-only
timed per whole command buffer:

| variant | N | GPU-total median (ms) | marginal (ms/dispatch) |
|---|---|---|---|
| shared | 28 | 5.842 | 0.2086 |
| rot8 (64MB set) | 28 | 5.757 | 0.2056 |
| **fresh (224MB, all cache-cold)** | 28 | 5.754 | **0.2055** |
| shared | 112 | 22.799 | 0.2036 |
| rot8 | 112 | 22.963 | 0.2050 |
| **fresh (896MB, all cache-cold)** | 112 | 23.071 | **0.2060** |
| shared-again (drift control) | 28 | 5.703 | 0.2037 |

**The amortization is IDENTICAL across all three variants** -- fresh, guaranteed-cache-cold
weights at every dispatch buy nothing back (0.2055-0.2060 vs 0.2036-0.2086; the spread is
within the 0.976 drift-control ratio). **Mechanism B (cache residency) is refuted outright.** The
amortization also cannot be weight-DRAM-bandwidth-bound: fresh-112 streams 896MB in 23.1ms = ~39
GB/s, trivial against the ~546 GB/s DRAM budget.

### Mechanism conclusion: temporal overlap / latency-hiding in the dense stream

With residency and (per Gate 0) CPU-encoding both excluded, the remaining explanation is that
consecutive llama.cpp dispatches OVERLAP in execution inside the batch: a lone dispatch runs
latency-dominated at ~2.9 TF/s (today's 0.747ms), while a dense stream keeps enough concurrent
work in flight to hide the latency and run the same kernel at aggregate ~10.5 TF/s. Same-day
same-session comparison, FLOPs = 2x256x1024x4096 = 2.147 GFLOP/dispatch, f16 MMA sustained wall
ceiling 13.3-14.0 TF/s:

| engine (format) | isolated GPU | batched GPU marginal | amortization | batched efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp `kernel_mul_mm_f16_f32` (F16) | 0.747 ms (2.9 TF/s) | **0.205 ms** | **3.6x** | **~10.5 TF/s ~= 77% of sustained f16 peak** |
| Algenta `_qkv_proj_gemm_mma8x8` (Int8) | 0.561 ms (3.8 TF/s) | **0.557 ms** | **1.01x (none)** | ~3.9 TF/s ~= 28% of f16 peak (and Int8 MMA ceilings at ~2x f16, so ~14% of its own format's ceiling) |

**The gap is NOT a scheduling trick we are missing at the command-buffer layer, NOT cache staging,
NOT tile shape / operand width / datatype (all refuted earlier in this tournament). It is MMA
micro-efficiency**: llama.cpp's kernel is latency-bound per dispatch and its dense stream hides the
latency to reach ~77% of sustained peak; Algenta's kernel runs at ~14% of its format ceiling in
EVERY context -- isolated, batched, today, Aug 7 -- which is the signature of an inner loop that
does not keep the MMA units fed (per-tile Int8 dequant + fragment shuffles on the critical path),
not of a kernel waiting for work that batching could supply.

### What this changes, and the pre-registered next experiment

- The "GEMM tournament round 2" scope the Phase 4 entry called for is re-scoped by this evidence:
  it is a MICROKERNEL-efficiency project (software-pipelined loads, deeper BK, fragment layout,
  moving dequant off the MMA critical path), not a dispatch-scheduling or cache-staging project.
  Comparable-scale undertaking, as the Phase 4 entry already warned.
- Pre-registered next experiment (cheap, decisive for attribution): a DUAL-STREAM concurrency
  test -- two queues committing N/2-dispatch batches simultaneously, aggregate GPU throughput vs
  the single-stream marginal. If aggregate throughput rises materially above single-stream, our
  kernel leaves occupancy headroom on the table (grid/fragment lever); if flat, the single-dispatch
  SIMD utilization is the floor and only the inner loop moves it. This doubles as the first probe
  of the campaign's concurrent-throughput axis.
- Files added (all additive): `mm_operator_harness_timestamped.m`, `mm_operator_harness_residency.m`
  (both in `benchmarks/competitors/llama_cpp/operator_harness/`); `mm_operator_harness_batched.m`
  from Gate 0 is bundled into the same PR (it was never committed). Re-run unmodified:
  `gemm_qkv_proj_batching_sim_gpuonly.mojo` + `batch_shim_gputime.m`.

## DUAL-STREAM CONCURRENCY TEST (2026-08-12): the attribution fork is CLOSED -- zero cross-stream overlap for BOTH kernels, aggregate throughput FALLS with concurrency; the GEMM lever is definitively inner-loop-only, and concurrent scaling must come from batched weight-sweeps, not concurrent streams

The "Gate 0, MECHANISM RESOLVED" entry pre-registered this experiment to split the remaining fork:
does `_qkv_proj_gemm_mma8x8` leave OCCUPANCY HEADROOM (two concurrent streams would raise
aggregate throughput -> a grid/fragment lever exists), or is its single-stream ~3.9 TF/s an
INNER-LOOP FLOOR (only a microkernel restructure moves it)? Built the commit/wait-split shim
(`batch_shim_async.m`: `algenta_commit_token_as` commits without waiting, `algenta_wait_token_as`
waits + returns GPUStartTime/GPUEndTime so the two-stream span and overlap are measured directly),
the Mojo probe `mma_forge/probes/gemm_qkv_proj_dualstream.mojo` (same plumbing/correctness-gate
convention as `gemm_qkv_proj_batching_sim_gpuonly.mojo`), and the identical-pairing ObjC control
`mm_operator_harness_dualstream.m` for llama.cpp's kernel.

### Algenta `_qkv_proj_gemm_mma8x8` (real qkv_proj shape, 15 reps/cell, medians)

| cell | median (ms) | marginal (ms/dispatch) | vs single |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 single N=112 | 62.801 | 0.5607 | baseline |
| S2 single N=56 | 32.082 | 0.5729 | (paired check) |
| D1 two streams x56 (112 total) | span 72.188 (durA 35.958 / durB 36.230) | 0.6445 | **0.87x** |
| D2 two streams x112 (224 total) | span 165.168 (durA 82.468 / durB 82.471) | 0.7374 | **0.76x** |

**Overlap is ZERO** -- D1 span (72.188) equals durA+durB (72.188) to four decimals; D2 the same
within 0.23ms. The two command buffers execute SERIALLY, and each stream runs ~12% SLOWER
co-scheduled (35.96/36.23 vs 32.08 single at N=56) -- concurrency is a pure loss here.

### llama.cpp `kernel_mul_mm_f16_f32` control (same session, same pairing)

| cell | median (ms) | marginal (ms/dispatch) | vs single |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 single N=112 | 18.160 | 0.1621 | baseline |
| S2 single N=56 | 9.186 | 0.1640 | (paired check) |
| D1 two streams x56 | span 19.368 (durA 9.659 / durB 9.687) | 0.1729 | **0.94x** |
| D2 two streams x112 | span 40.273 (durA 20.068 / durB 20.145) | 0.1798 | 0.90x |

**The control shows the SAME signature**: zero overlap across command buffers (span == durA+durB
within 0.03ms) and aggregate throughput slightly BELOW single-stream. Two consequences:
1. **llama.cpp's 3.6x batch amortization happens INSIDE one command buffer/encoder** (dispatches
   pipelining against each other within a single dense stream), NOT across streams -- cross-stream
   concurrency buys nothing even for the kernel that benefits most from intra-stream overlap.
2. This session's single-stream marginal (0.162ms = ~13.3 TF/s) sits essentially AT the sustained
   f16 MMA wall (13.3-14.0 TF/s) -- the earlier same-day residency session measured 0.204-0.209ms;
   the GPU clock state drifted again within the day (their latency-sensitive kernel tracks it, our
   kernel does not: 0.557-0.561 both sessions). Same-session ratios remain the valid axis; the
   cross-session absolute drift is disclosed, not smoothed.

### Verdict (per the pre-registered rule) and what it closes

Aggregate speedup was required to be >= 1.15x for "occupancy headroom"; measured 0.87x (Algenta)
and 0.94x (control) -- **VERDICT: INNER-LOOP FLOOR, confirmed**. The attribution fork from the
mechanism-resolution entry is closed with direct measurement:
- There is NO grid/fragment/occupancy lever for `_qkv_proj_gemm_mma8x8`: its 1024-threadgroup x
  256-thread grid already fills the machine (262K threads in flight); a second stream cannot
  interleave and only steals cycles.
- There is also NO concurrent-stream lever for serving throughput at the GEMM level, for ANY
  kernel on this machine: even peak-efficiency streams serialize across command buffers. The
  campaign's concurrent-throughput axis stays where the Slipstream work already put it --
  BATCHING (one weight sweep amortized over B sequences), not concurrent dispatch streams.
- The remaining 2.7x-class GEMM gap is exclusively inner-loop MMA issue efficiency (per-tile Int8
  dequant + fragment shuffles on the critical path, ~14% of the Int8 ceiling vs llama.cpp's ~77%
  of f16 peak in-stream). "GEMM tournament round 2" is therefore confirmed as a microkernel
  project: software-pipelined loads, deeper BK, fragment layout, dequant off the MMA critical
  path. Comparable-scale undertaking, now with no remaining ambiguity about where the lever is.

Files added (all additive): `benchmarks/llm_smoke/metal_batch_dispatch/batch_shim_async.m`,
`mma_forge/probes/gemm_qkv_proj_dualstream.mojo`, `benchmarks/competitors/llama_cpp/
operator_harness/mm_operator_harness_dualstream.m`. Existing files untouched.

## CONCURRENT AXIS, FIRST 3-WAY BATCHED RACE (2026-08-12): Algenta's shipped Slipstream batched decode BEATS its own serial behavior 2.77x at B=32 but LOSES to llama.cpp's slot batching 1.68x-2.26x -- the limiter is the per-sequence part of the batched step, NOT the GEMMs

New harness `concurrent_3way.py` (this directory): B prompts in flight at once, aggregate SYSTEM
decode tok/s, each engine measured doing its OWN production concurrent thing -- Algenta
`decode_batched()` (one call, B sequences, Slipstream one-weight-sweep-per-token path, SDK-
exposed) vs Algenta B sequential single-stream `decode()` calls (internal control) vs llama.cpp B
concurrent `/completion` requests against ONE resident `llama-server --parallel 32` (its slot-
based continuous batching) vs MLX-LM B sequential generations (its honest story: no server, no
batching). B in {8, 16, 32}, in=264 tokens (whole-unit prompts, distinct per sequence, shared
bytes/tokenizer across engines), out=128, greedy, untimed warmup at the exact timed shape per
engine per cell, rotating engine order, 45s inter-engine cooldowns, 2 passes, medians. Env note:
the SDK needs the documented dev knobs to resolve the local worker (ALGENTA_NATIVE_WORKER +
ALGENTA_RUNTIME_FALLBACK_MODE=allow) -- the harness's first launch attempt died on exactly this
and the usage block now states it.

| B | algenta-batched | algenta-serial | llama.cpp concurrent | mlx-lm serial |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 216.8 | 176.9 | **489.6** | 183.6 |
| 16 | 360.0 | 197.8 | **588.8** | 129.6 |
| 32 | 540.4 | 195.3 | **909.7** | 134.1 |

(system decode tok/s, medians of 2 passes; precisions as shipped: algenta int8, llama.cpp F16,
mlx-lm bf16)

**VERDICT, stated plainly: this axis is a LOSS against llama.cpp today** (2.26x behind at B=8,
1.64x at B=16, 1.68x at B=32). Two things are simultaneously true and both matter:
1. Batched decode is REAL for us: 540.4 vs 195.3 system tok/s at B=32 = 2.77x over our own
   serial behavior, and batched scales while serial is flat (176.9/197.8/195.3 across B) -- the
   Slipstream weight-sweep amortization works through the full SDK path, as engine-internal
   benches predicted.
2. But OUR scaling is sublinear: B x4 (8->32) buys only 2.49x throughput, while llama.cpp's
   slot batching buys 1.86x over the same range and lands at 909.7. Their per-request decode
   median falls 91.3 -> 38.8 tok/s across B while system throughput CLIMBS -- their scheduler
   keeps amortizing the weight sweep across slots far past where ours does.

**Per-step arithmetic pinning the limiter** (same-session, engine-reported): at B=32 our engine
system rate 540.4 tok/s means one batched step (all 32 sequences advance one token) takes
32/540.4 = ~59 ms. A single-stream decode step on this same worker is ~3.6-3.8 ms (~263-277
tok/s, the serial lane's pass-1 per-sequence rate). The Phase-3 M-sweep already proved the
batched GEMM cost at m_rows=32 is ~1.1 ms per step (the per-token GEMM collapse to the compute
floor). So of the ~59 ms batched step, GEMM is ~1-2 ms: the remaining ~57 ms lives in the
PER-SEQUENCE part of the step -- batched per-seq decode attention (the split-K partial+merge
pair over B=32 growing KV caches at depth ~264-390), per-seq KV writes/quant, and the
descriptor/dispatch structure around them -- NOT in the projections. The dual-stream entry's
conclusion (concurrency comes from batched weight-sweeps, never concurrent streams) is confirmed
on the GEMM side and now sharpened: the sweep amortizes, the per-sequence attention tail does
not, and that tail is where llama.cpp's slot batching still beats us.

**Caveats, disclosed:** 2-pass medians are fragile -- the serial lane swung 277.1 -> 176.9 at
B=8 across passes (thermal state after a full day of sustained GPU work today), and mlx-lm's
B=16 median (129.6) came from one anomalously slow pass (129.6 vs 205.6). The LOSS verdict does
not depend on any fragile number: llama.cpp leads every engine at every B by >= 1.6x with
separated distributions. MLX's lane is sequential BY DESIGN (it ships no server); its numbers
state that honestly, they are not a batching failure. Per the standing no-loss-pages rule, this
stays ledger-internal until the axis flips.

**Pre-registered next experiment** (before any kernel change): a `step_batched` counter probe at
B=32 (existing GPU-counter probe pattern, batched descriptor table) splitting that ~59 ms step
into attention-partial / attention-merge / kvprod / GEMM / lm_head / dispatch-gap buckets, the
same way the Phase-4 operator-differential table split prefill. The bucket that owns the ~57 ms
names the round-3 target.

## CONCURRENT AXIS, ROUND 2 -- THE COUNTER PROBE REFUTES OUR OWN SUBTRACTION DIAGNOSIS (2026-08-12): the batched step's limiter is SMALL-M GEMM UNDERFILL (31 ms, B-independent) + an under-parallelized batched lm_head (10 ms at B=32), NOT the per-sequence attention tail

Owner pushback ("you are doing something completely wrong... we are missing some crucial
components, heavy delay") triggered the pre-registered counter probe EARLY: new probe
`qwen3_probe_counters_decode_batched.mojo` (this directory; campaign counter-shim pattern,
per-dispatch hardware timestamps over the session's OWN `descriptors_decode_batched` table,
tick rate calibrated, 5 samples, medians). Synthetic uniform depth=300 state (timing is
shape-driven, value-independent).

### Measured per-role GPU totals for ONE batched step

| role | B=32 (ms) | B=1 (ms) | scaling |
|---|---|---|---|
| qkv_gemm (28 dispatches) | 6.61 (0.236 ea) | 6.31 | B-INDEPENDENT |
| swiglu_gemm | 9.28 (0.331 ea) | 9.10 | B-INDEPENDENT |
| down_proj_accum | 9.03 (0.323 ea) | 8.17 | B-INDEPENDENT |
| o_proj_accum | 6.15 (0.220 ea) | 5.51 | B-INDEPENDENT |
| **GEMM subtotal** | **31.07** | **29.09** | ~flat -> LATENCY-BOUND |
| lmhead_batched (1 dispatch) | **10.15** | 0.69 | ~15x for 32x rows |
| attn_PARTIAL | 4.81 (0.178 ea) | 0.57 | ~B-scaling |
| kvprod_batched | 0.82 | 0.33 | mild |
| attn_merge / norms / embed / argmax | ~0.9 | ~0.5 | small |
| GPU-sum | 47.72 | 31.22 | |
| wall median | 55.81 | 40.59 | |
| wall-GPU gap (256 dispatches) | 8.08 | 9.37 | dispatch overhead |

**CORRECTION to the round-1 entry's subtraction diagnosis**: "GEMM is ~1-2 ms of the ~59 ms
step (Phase-3 M-sweep proven)" is WRONG for this path. The M-sweep's ~7.3 TF/s-at-M=32 figure
came from `msl_batchsweep_bench.m`'s own configuration; the ACTUAL in-step MSL-parity GEMM
dispatches at m_rows<=32 run 0.22-0.33 ms EACH. Mechanism, read off the table: the prefill-tuned
MSL-parity kernels' geometry (NR1=32 rows x NR0=64 cols per threadgroup) caps the grid at
(M/32) x (N/64) threadgroups -- at M<=32 that is 16 (o_proj/down), 16 (o), 64 (qkv), 96 (swiglu)
threadgroups of 128 threads = 2-12% of a 40-core GPU. Every GEMM is latency-bound at ~1-3%
machine occupancy, and adding rows up to one full M-tile (B<=32) costs almost nothing -- hence
the ~30 ms B-INDEPENDENT fixed cost the round-1 fit found but could not name. The batched lm_head
(Option B) is the second component: one dispatch sweeps 155 MB of vocab weights for all B rows,
but its `_LM_BLOCKS`-sized grid gives it ~10.1 ms at B=32 (~1 TF/s effective; bandwidth floor is
~0.3 ms; at B=1 it is 0.69 ms) -- B rows of accumulator work serialized through too few
threadgroups. Attention's 4.8 ms is real but THIRD.

**Everything now reconciles**: round-1's fitted F=29.5 ms fixed + 0.93 ms/seq == GEMM-underfill
(fixed) + attention/kvprod/lmhead (B-scaling). The "heavy delay" is not one thing: it is (1)
running prefill-geometry GEMMs at decode batch sizes, (2) an lm_head grid sized for B=1-era
workloads, (3) 256-dispatch per-step overhead (~8 ms), in descending order.

**The fix this names (round-3 scope, next)**: small-M GEMM geometry for the batched decode table
-- split-K across the K axis to multiply threadgroups (the campaign ALREADY built exactly this for
single-stream decode: `msl_splitk_accum.metal`, S=8/S=12 partials + atomic accumulate, proven
1.32-1.34x standalone at M=1); raise lm_head parallelism (more blocks, less serial per-block
work); then re-measure. Ceiling estimate if GEMM reaches its M-sweep efficiency and lm_head its
bandwidth floor: ~12-15 ms/step at B=32 -> ~2,100-2,600 system tok/s, ~2.5x llama.cpp's 910.
Probe file + build recipe committed alongside this entry.

## CONCURRENT AXIS, ROUND 3 INCREMENT 1 LANDED (2026-08-12): split-K MSL GEMMs wired into the batched decode table -- o_proj 9.6x, down_proj 11.9x faster; batched step 55.8->42.0ms at B=32; the B=32 race reaches PARITY with llama.cpp (788 vs 807 system tok/s = 0.98x, was 0.59x)

The round-2 counter probe named the limiter (small-M GEMM underfill); this is the first fix. The
batched decode table ran the plain Mojo accum GEMM for o_proj/down_proj at m_rows=B<=32 -- grid
(M/32)x(N/32)=16 threadgroups, ~2% of the GPU. Wired in the SAME split-K substitution
`_apply_m_rows_af_nomirror` already uses for the single-stream path: `msl_splitk8` (o_proj, S=8:
16x8=128 threadgroups) and `msl_splitk12` (down_proj, S=12: 16x12=192), atomic-float-add partials
(residual-safe "+=", no zeroing), same shape gates (n_q%256==0 / d_ff%384==0), F16 weight twins.

TWO wiring bugs caught by the token-identity validation BEFORE any timing was trusted (both
produced the degenerate 374-repeat stream): (1) the MSL split-K kernels read the F16 weight twins
-- arg 2 must swap to `msl_w_o/down_f16_addr` exactly as the nomirror path does under
`use_msl_accum`; passing the Int8 originals corrupts the products. (2) MSL tiles are 32x64: the
grid must use `_ceil_div(N, 64)` (NOT `_GEMM_BN`=32, which doubles the grid and lets the MSL
kernel's unguarded tiles run past N into adjacent memory) and the dispatch must use 128 threads
(the kernels' `max_total_threads_per_threadgroup`), NOT `_GEMM_NTHREADS`=256. Post-fix validation:
decode_batched(B=4, 24 steps) == serial == official worker, all four prompts, oracle continuation
[374, 12095, 13, 576, ...] intact; cross-worker serial byte-identical.

Counter probe at B=32, depth=300 (per-role medians, ms): o_proj 6.15 -> 0.64 (9.6x), down_proj
9.03 -> 0.76 (11.9x); step wall 55.8 -> 42.0 ms, GPU-sum 47.7 -> 33.6 ms. GEMM subtotal now 17.2
ms (qkv 6.59 + swiglu 9.26 still unfixed + o/down 1.4); lm_head 9.88; attn 4.74; gap 8.5.

Re-race (same harness/protocol, 2 passes, medians; worker algenta-gpu-worker-dbsplitk):

| 16 | 360.0 | 576.8 | 691.8 | 0.83x |
| 32 | 540.4 | 788.4 | 807.3 | **0.98x (parity)** |

## Parametric d_head -- the model-agnostic mandate increment (2026-08-13)

**What changed.** `_MBQwen3I8AllSimd7Prefill` no longer refuses every `d_head != 128`. It now
accepts any **power-of-two `d_head` up to `RESIDENT_MAX_HEAD_DIM` (256)** and routes a non-128
model onto the engine's already-validated runtime-parametric path: plan resolution gates
`af_grouped_fa_available` on `d_head == _AF_STRUCTURAL_D_HEAD`, so a d_head != 128 request for the
fast attention-forge plan degrades to `PF_ATTN_OFF` (prefill attention `_pf_attn_tiled_kernel_simd`
+ legacy `_sdpa_kernel_simd` decode, both parametric for power-of-two d_head <= 256) instead of
computing wrong attention. d_head == 128 keeps the exact fast path -- the gate adds a literal
`and True`, byte-for-byte unchanged. The prior blanket refusal (2026-08-12 audit) is superseded;
only what genuinely cannot run is still refused, loudly and by name: `d_head > 256` (parametric
shared-mem ceiling) and non-power-of-two d_head (the residentk reduction is not validated for it).

**Why.** The owner mandate: "never hardcode values -- must work on any Qwen/other LLM model." The
fast AF kernels (steel prefill comptime `_D=128`, kvprod_v3/f4u2/i8kv one-simdgroup lane-x4) are
structurally 128; the engine has always ALSO carried the parametric path, so the honest fix is
routing, not a silent hardcode or a blanket refusal.

**Verification (same session, M4 Max, worker `algenta-gpu-worker-dhead` rebuilt from this tree on
Mojo 1.0.0b2).** `tests/test_inference_gpu_e2e.py`: **6 passed, 1 skipped** -- the campaign oracle
(`test_sdk_decode_06b_matches_campaign_oracle`, first token 374 + byte-identical continuation),
long-generation-past-512, quantized-cache token-identity, and sampling greedy-equivalence/
determinism all green; the skip is the 1.7B test (needs the separate stage-6144 worker). Decisive
for the no-regression claim: the d_head=128 decode ran at **199 dispatches/token -- the documented
AF-nomirror-MSL production budget -- i.e. the FAST path was dispatched, not the degraded parametric
one**, and the rebuilt worker's recorded source hash is byte-identical to the committed
`session_prefill.mojo`. The standalone session test at d_head=32 now gets PAST construction
(previously the blanket refusal raised there), confirming the constructor accepts a non-128
power-of-two head dim.

**Honest scope.** Every Qwen3 checkpoint is d_head=128, so this unlocks no NEW model today -- it is
mandate-compliance: the engine is now correct-by-routing for any power-of-two d_head <= 256 rather
than hardcoded/refusing. The architecture gates (GQA, QK-norm, tied embeddings) still bound the
supported FAMILY to Qwen3; llama-family support is separate work. Remaining follow-ups for full
any-model: a d_head != 128 end-to-end oracle (needs a non-Qwen3 checkpoint or a synthetic-weight
gate), and eventually structural parametric versions of the AF kernels themselves so a non-128 model
gets a fast path, not just a correct one. No performance change at d_head=128 (the fast path is
untouched by construction).

## Llama-family support, increment 1 -- SDK foundation (2026-08-13)

First increment toward running architectures beyond Qwen3 (the model-agnostic mandate's next
frontier; the full blocker map is dissected in the campaign memory). This one is deliberately the
SAFE, additive foundation -- no gate that guards against silently-wrong math is relaxed yet.

**What changed (SDK, `algenta.inference`):**
- `_normalize_config()` derives `head_dim = hidden_size // num_attention_heads` when a config omits
  it (the llama-family convention). An already-present `head_dim` is always trusted, never re-derived
  -- correct because Qwen3's explicit `head_dim` (128) is NOT `hidden_size/num_attention_heads`
  (64); its q/k/v project to `h_q*head_dim`. This clears the FIRST llama refusal (missing `head_dim`).
- `prepare_model_checkpoint` now carries the checkpoint's own `eos_token_id` into the manifest config
  (written only when present), preparing the replacement of the engine's hardcoded Qwen3 EOS constant.

**What is deliberately NOT done yet** (each would be silently-wrong without its engine half): the
tied-embeddings gate stays (no separate lm_head path yet), and q/k_norm are still required (no
QK-norm skip in the kernels yet). Those land with their engine/kernel changes.

**Verification:** `tests/test_inference_model_agnostic.py` 10 passed / 1 skipped (the two new
`_normalize_config` tests + all pre-existing gates); Qwen3 GPU e2e `tests/test_inference_gpu_e2e.py`
6 passed / 1 skipped -- the change is a byte-for-byte no-op for Qwen3 (head_dim present and trusted,
eos carried), oracle token 374 intact.

## Llama-family support -- Algenta runs a llama-architecture model end-to-end (2026-08-13)

The any-model mandate's flagship milestone: the engine now runs a NON-Qwen3 architecture. Target:
**TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0** (Apache-2.0, ungated; model_type=llama, NO head_dim field,
tie_word_embeddings=false, NO q_norm/k_norm, eos=2, rope_theta=10000, d_head=64, d_ff=5632).

**What landed (across #664 + this change):**
- SDK: `_normalize_config` derives `head_dim=hidden_size//num_attention_heads` when a config omits it
  (llama convention; an explicit head_dim is always trusted -- Qwen3's is NOT that formula). Detects
  `has_qk_norm` from the safetensors and carries it + `tie_word_embeddings` + `eos_token_id` into the
  manifest. Branches the tied-embeddings gate (untied now accepted) and makes q/k_norm tensors
  conditional. lm_head.weight is converted for untied models.
- Engine: a `qk_norm` flag on the three parametric-path ropewrt kernels (`_qk_rope_write_kernel`,
  `_kvf16`, `_pf_ropewrt_kernel`) -- 1 = Qwen3 RMSNorm-then-RoPE, 0 = llama rotate-the-raw-projection
  (never reads the absent norm gains); wired at every dispatch of those kernels. An untied model gets
  a separate int8 lm_head buffer pair (tied aliases it onto embed = zero extra memory); the ~12
  lm_head/logits descriptor sites repoint to it. No-QK-norm models are gated off the attention-forge
  blobs (`af_grouped_fa_available and qk_norm == 1`) and route to the runtime-parametric path
  (PF_ATTN_OFF prefill + legacy decode) that parametric d_head (#663) already opened -- d_head=64
  lands there. Entry points read the flags + EOS and stop on the model's own eos_token_id.
- Staging: TinyLlama's d_ff=5632 > the 3072 default tier, so the worker builds with
  ALGENTA_STAGE_6144 (the same per-model staging tier Qwen3-1.7B uses).

**Verification (same session, M4 Max):**
- Qwen3 REGRESSION first: `tests/test_inference_gpu_e2e.py` 6 passed / 1 skipped, oracle token 374
  intact, on the llama-capable worker -- the production path is untouched (qk_norm=1, tied).
- TinyLlama vs an INDEPENDENT transformers CPU reference (FP32, torch 2.5.1): prompt "The capital of
  Germany is" -> Algenta `[5115, 29892, 607, 338, 884, 278]` == CPU `[5115, 29892, 607, 338, 884, 278]`
  **byte-for-byte all 6 tokens**; prompt "The capital of France is" -> first 3 tokens exact
  (`3900, 29889, 13` = " Paris.\n"), then an expected int8-vs-FP32 near-tie divergence in the
  repetitive continuation (same trade documented for quantized Qwen3). Greedy-deterministic across
  runs and cold/warm cache loads; 179.8 decode tok/s.

**Honest scope / residual gap:** the repo tokenizer is Qwen3-only (rejects llama's SentencePiece
normalizer), so llama serving is token-id prompts until that parity item lands; TinyLlama is a chat
model, so the raw question form trips its template into an early EOS (statement prompts used). The
attention-forge FAST path still assumes QK-norm/d_head=128 -- a llama d_head=128 model (e.g. 3.x 8B)
runs correct on the parametric path but not the fast path yet. Remaining for full parity: llama-family
tokenizer, rope_scaling (llama-3.1+), and AF-blob QK-norm variants for the llama d_head=128 fast path.

First llama-on-llama.cpp race (TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, M4 Max, llama.cpp build 10210 Metal,
converted F16 GGUF from the SAME safetensors Algenta ran + a q8_0 quant for the quant-matched arm):

| Arm | TinyLlama decode tok/s | prefill (pp512) |
|---|---|---|
| Algenta int8 (steady-state, 3 runs) | 174 | (6-tok prompt, n/a) |
| llama.cpp F16 | ~192 (189.9/194.1) | ~6580 |
| llama.cpp Q8_0 (quant-matched) | ~302 | ~6260 |

## feat/gemv-streaming -- GEMV weight-streaming overhaul lifts TinyLlama 174->289 tok/s (1.64x), Qwen3 +15% (2026-08-13)

CORRECTS the previous entry's diagnosis. The GPU-counter profile (tinyllama_probe_counters_decode)
showed GEMV projections = 87.6% of per-token GPU time and Algenta int8 streaming at only ~181 GB/s
(33% of the M4 Max ~546 GB/s ceiling) while moving HALF the bytes llama.cpp F16 moves -- so the gap
WAS kernel efficiency in the decode GEMV triple, not (only) the attention path. Branch
`feat/gemv-streaming` rebuilt the int8 decode GEMV kernels in `residentk/kernels.mojo`:

1. DE-STAGING (the big one). Every fused GEMV kernel staged the k-length input vector into a
   `_STAGE` shared `stack_allocation` so the 8 output columns could share it. `stack_allocation` size
   is fixed per pipeline-state object, so TinyLlama (`d_ff=5632` -> `-D ALGENTA_STAGE_6144`) pinned
   ALL of them at 24 KiB threadgroup memory = ONE resident threadgroup per core. A decode GEMV is
   weight-streaming bound (n*k int8 bytes streamed, the k-vector touched once per row), so the
   staging copy was a rounding error of traffic buying a 4-8x occupancy hit. Removed it: the
   o_proj/down_proj accum kernel reads x straight from device (was a plain copy, bit-for-bit); the
   norm + gate/up + lm_head kernels apply `(x*inv)*gamma` on the fly with the SAME left-to-right
   Float32 expression the staging loop evaluated (every staged value reproduced bit-for-bit). Shared
   drops from 24 KiB to 32-64 bytes/TG; the lm_head argmax/logits pair de-staged too.
2. FUSED GATE/UP SWIGLU into one pass (two register accumulators, one x/gamma stream, dropped the
   mid-kernel barrier + gsh handoff). Largest single role.
3. ORDER-PRESERVING UNROLLS. Two-step unroll across all GEMV dot loops (both steps' loads in flight
   before either is consumed, additions still in step order); the o_proj/down_proj accum loop went to
   FOUR steps. Every per-lane partial sum stays bit-for-bit, so the greedy sequence is unchanged.
4. RE-MEASURED `_TG` with the occupancy ceiling gone: 512 (16 cols/TG) LOST ~4%, 128 tied, 256 kept.

MEASURED (harness `benchmarks/llm_smoke/tinyllama_gemv_bench.py`, warmup + median-of-3, interleaved
baseline/variant same session; TinyLlama-1.1B int8, France prompt, 128 new tokens):
  * baseline (worker `-llama`): 174.7/175.8/175.9 -> ~175 tok/s
  * de-staging only: 238 tok/s (1.36x)
  * + fused swiglu: 265 tok/s
  * + unrolls + 4-step accum: FINAL 288.1/288.7/290.8 -> ~289 tok/s = 1.64x baseline
  Per-role GPU-counter before->after (n_keys=7): qkv 0.83->0.50ms, o_proj 0.55->0.30, swiglu
  2.32->1.25, down_proj 1.37->0.65, lm_head 0.26->0.18; GEMV subtotal 5.07->2.69ms. Implied
  weight-streaming bandwidth on the big roles now ~390-410 GB/s (was ~181 aggregate).

CORRECTNESS: greedy output byte-identical to baseline across every variant and run (first tokens
[3900,29889,13,...], full 128-token periodic sequence). Qwen3-0.6B regression: test_inference_gpu_e2e
6 passed / 1 skipped, oracle token 374 + long-gen + sampling all green -- and the SAME kernels lifted
Qwen3-0.6B single-stream decode 301->346 tok/s (+15%, interleaved A/B), so the shared-kernel change is
a win there too (the stale `< 330` throughput ceiling in that test raised to `< 420` with the floor
untouched). Kernel-level suite test_residentk_gemv_simd_kernel.mojo does not compile on this pinned
toolchain on origin/main either (DeviceContext.enqueue_function_unchecked API drift) -- pre-existing,
not caused by this change; the e2e oracle gates above carry the correctness evidence.

HONEST REMAINDER: 289 still trails llama.cpp Q8_0's ~302 by ~4%. The probe's shallow-depth floor is
~304-306 tok/s; the e2e number averages over the growing context (n_keys 7->134 crosses into the deep
split-K table at >=32, where attention grows). The remaining gap is attention/context-scaling and
host/dispatch overhead, NOT the GEMV weight stream -- the GEMV triple now runs at ~390-410 GB/s, above
llama.cpp Q8_0's ~314 GB/s aggregate. REFUTED on the way (measured, not retried): prefetching the first
unrolled step across the norm reduction (register pressure, -1%); 4-step unroll on the norm/swiglu
kernels (register pressure, ~-3%, kept 2-step there); 16-columns-per-TG (_TG=512, -4%); 128-bit
reinterpreted int8 loads (never built -- lane-assignment changes break the byte-identical summation
order, and the 32-bit manual-bitcast ancestor was already refuted).

NOTE: the earlier "FIX PLAN" above (no-QK-norm AF KV-producer blob + d_head=64 split-K) is the
COMPLEMENTARY next lever for deep-context llama decode (attention is ~22% of the step at 1K keys);
this entry closed the GEMV weight-streaming gap that dominated short-context decode.

## feat/llama-native-deep -- llama DECODE gets the native fast path: deep-context +20% @1K keys (2026-08-13)

The "FIX PLAN" from the two entries above is LANDED. TinyLlama (llama arch, d_head=64, GQA 32:4,
no QK-norm, untied) now routes onto the packed-F16 native KV + flash-decoding split-K DECODE path
that was previously hardwired to d_head=128 + QK-norm (Qwen3-only). Prefill attention stays the
runtime-parametric OFF family (the steel grouped-FA kernel is structural d_head=128); the KV
contract is consistent by construction: the new plan's prefill table DOUBLE-WRITES (parametric
`_pf_ropewrt_kernel` populates the natural F32 cache prefill attention reads; the AF native-KV-
producer populates the packed F16 native cache decode reads) and derives
`DECODE_PATH_NATIVE_PACKED_KV`, so prefill-time writes and decode-time reads can never disagree.

WHAT LANDED
- `native_kv_producer` blob grew the trailing llama-family `qk_norm` flag (1 = Qwen3 RMSNorm-then-
  RoPE, byte-identical to the pre-flag math; 0 = llama rotate-the-raw-projection, never reads
  qn_w/kn_w) -- same pattern #665's residentk kernels use. Blob regenerated.
- NEW d_head=64 split-K decode partial (`attention_forge/native_kv_decode_attn_splitk_f2.mojo`):
  one 32-lane simdgroup per (head, split), two head-elements per lane, single simd_sum per key,
  same (m,l,o) contract as f4u2 so the engine merge is untouched. Plain f2 and 2-key-unrolled f2u2
  both written; interleaved e2e A/B shipped f2u2 (1.086x f2 at 1024 keys: median 267.5 vs 246.3,
  byte-identical greedy; ~+3% at 256) -- exactly the f4/f4u2 precedent of the 128 blob.
- NEW plan `PF_ATTN_PARAMETRIC_NATIVE_DECODE` (+ `KV_CONTRACT_MIRRORED_NATIVE_DECODE`): a
  `PF_ATTN_GROUPED_FA_NO_MIRROR` request whose structural-128/QK-norm gate fails now degrades
  CLOSEST-CAPABILITY-FIRST onto this plan before bare OFF. Engine: new pnat prefill table (OFF
  table + kvprod dispatch), d_head-resolved effective split-K partial (f4u2 @128, f2u2 @64, none
  otherwise -> naive native decode), i8kv/batched tables gated to structural d_head=128.
- `MB_MAX_ARGS` raised 16 -> 17 (ffi.mojo + both shims) -- the kvprod dispatches bind the qk_norm
  flag as their 17th arg. Model-parametric throughout: derived from dims + discovered pipelines,
  never a model name.

Probe wall matches the e2e harness within ~1% at both depths (290.2/268.1 in the #669 entry),
so the probe is production-faithful. TWO profile verdicts set the lever search:
  * DISPATCH GAP IS ZERO: wall <= GPU-sum at both depths -- host encoding is fully overlapped
    behind GPU execution. The "dispatch/host overhead" hypothesis from the #669 residual
    estimate is REFUTED by measurement; llama.cpp's MTLDispatchTypeConcurrent is NOT a lever
    here (we run 157 dispatches/token vs their ~515-540, already fully pipelined).
  * ATTENTION GROWS WITH DEPTH: partial 0.34 ms @288 -> 0.60 ms @1056 (+ merge 0.12 flat),
    while GEMV/kvprod/tail stay flat. The deep residual is attention.

LEVER SEARCH (all at production shape h_q=32/h_kv=4/d_head=64/kbs=32, interleaved medians):
  * n_splits sweep @1056: 16 = optimal. 32: partial 0.60 (tied) but merge 0.12->0.18; 64:
    partial 0.72, merge 0.28. REFUTED (matches the Qwen3-era sweep's "above the TG-count
    optimum loses" finding at d_head=64 too).
  * MUTANT DISSECTION of the f2u2 partial (25.9 us/dispatch @1056): no-shuffle mutant -1.6%,
    no-exp mutant -2.1%, NO-LOADS mutant -41% (10.7 us) -> K/V MEMORY ACCESS is 59% of the
    kernel; a key-major-K-addressing mutant recovers 1.25x. Root cause: the packed K layout is
    ELEMENT-major inside a block (`K[hk][block][e][kk]`), so f2u2's per-key strided scalar K
    loads (2 useful bytes per 64-byte line, ~3% utilization, amplified by GQA 8 q-heads
    re-reading each kv head) are the cost. Shuffle/exp compute is NOT the bottleneck.
  * KEY-SIMD (vectorize scores across keys + SIMD warp-shuffle reduction): IMPOSSIBLE on this
    nightly -- `std.gpu.primitives.warp.shuffle_xor` rejects every SIMD width but 1
    ("Unsupported simd_width" for 2/4/8), so multi-key reductions cannot share a shuffle chain.
  * REGISTER-BLOCKED staging (f2r8/f2r16: width-8/16 SIMD K loads staged, then consumed):
    BIT-EXACT but 0.79-0.85x -- SIMD-register extraction spills eat the load gain. REFUTED.
  * WIDTH-8 staging (f2s8, constant-index unroll): 1.01-1.06x. REFUTED (the width-4 unroll is
    the sweet spot; wider staging loses on register pressure/scheduling).
  * THE WINNER, f2s4 (`attention_forge/native_kv_decode_attn_splitk_f2s4.mojo`): stage the next
    4 keys' K as two WIDTH-4 SIMD loads per lane (contiguous ACROSS keys = full-line streaming
    within the 32-key block), consume them with EXACTLY f2's per-key scalar arithmetic in key
    order (constant SIMD-index extracts; lead-in aligns kk to 4, odd tail runs the f2 body).
    Standalone race (median-of-9 interleaved, per dispatch): 1.00x f2u2 @288 keys (13.6 vs
    13.7 us), 1.30x @1056 (19.9 vs 26.0 us), 1.48x @2048 (27.1 vs 40.2 us) -- the gain grows
    with depth exactly where the Q8_0 gap grows.
  * kvprod lever (0.21 ms/token = 9.6 us/layer, ~2x the 4.5-5 us dispatch floor): lane-fused
    no-QK-norm twin `kvprod_f1` (each lane owns its whole RoPE pair -> no shared scratch, no
    barrier, d_head/2 threads). BIT-EXACT at every pos_base (mid-block, block-boundary, deep)
    but standalone 1.005x -> REFUTED as a perf lever (the cost is launch-floor dominated, not
    scratch/barrier); NOT wired into the engine. Module + drivers committed as evidence.

WHAT LANDED
  * `native_kv_decode_attn_splitk_f2s4.mojo` + blob driver + regenerated blob
    (`generated/native_kv_decode_attn_splitk_f2s4_blob.c`); A/B family + bit-exact gate in
    `native_kv_decode_attn_splitk_f2r{,_driver}.mojo` (worst-abs-diff vs f2u2 = 0.0 on m/l/o

## BATCHED (CONCURRENT) SERVING FOR LLAMA -- feat/batched-llama (2026-08-14, branch feat/batched-llama)

The batched decode tier was gated qk_norm==1 / structural d_head=128 (the batched kvprod blob
applied the Qwen3 QK-norm unconditionally; the batched split-K partial blob is the f4u2 family,
block_dim = d_head//4 = 16 lanes at d64 = half a SIMD group). GENERALIZED to llama d_head=64 /
qk_norm=0 (TinyLlama), mirroring the single-stream llama pattern (#669/#672):

- kvprod_batched grows the trailing qk_norm flag (1 = Qwen3 RMSNorm-then-RoPE, byte-for-byte the
  pre-flag math; 0 = llama rotate-raw, qn_w/kn_w never read). Standalone driver: bit-exact (0.0
  worst ratio) vs the single-stream twin on d64 h32/h4 ragged poss + d128 qk0 control.
- NEW attention_forge/native_kv_decode_attn_splitk_bf2.mojo: the d64 BATCHED partial (bf2u2 =
  batched twin of single-stream f2u2: one simdgroup, 2 elems/lane, same batched indirection as the
  d128 f4u2 blob). Standalone driver: oracle worst-ratio <= 0.018 (f16 bound) incl ragged/empty-
  split, cross-check vs B single-stream f2u2 dispatches <= 1.4e-3 (merge f32-vs-f64 noise). AIR
  name native_kv_decode_attn_splitk_bf2_<hex> verified on the forged blob; engine discovery is a
  new elif in the six-way longest-first splitk chain + a d_head-resolved batched-partial eff slot
  (d128 -> _bat f4u2 at d_head//4 threads byte-for-byte as before; d64+qk0 -> bf2u2 at 32).
- decode_batched_built no longer blanket d128+qk1 -- it is eff-slot + four-roles discovered; the
  family pairing (d128 both families; d64 requires qk0) is enforced by the same gate.
- prefill_batch_batched_ingest accepts the naive-producer AF table (llama) and retargets the RIGHT
  kvprod cache-pointer args per table variant (v2 pair: arg0/1; naive producer: arg1/2 -- arg0 is
  q_native there; patching 0/1 would have pointed q_native at the batched K cache).
- Merge/batched-lm_head/argmax tail already d_head-parametric + norm-agnostic; the batched lm_head
  reads self.lm_head_addr, so untied llama lm_heads work with zero extra wiring.

TWO LATENT BATCHED-TABLE BUGS FOUND+FIXED (both invisible while every batched model stayed on the
MSL split-K arms; both exposed by the first llama batched session):
1. msl_splitk4__swiglu_partial_f16_f32's atomic epilogue wrote ALL 32 staged rows into the
   B-sized scratch with no m_abs < M guard = OOB GPU write at every B < 32. Qwen3 survived by
   LUCK (the logits buffer allocated right after mapped the whole OOB reach; zero-valued atomic
   adds are value-neutral where mapped). TinyLlama's ~1.4MB reach past an 88KB scratch hit
   unmapped pages -> GPU hang, then page fault (proven by descriptor prefix-bisection: [0,11) ok,
   [0,12) hangs; the apply kernel alone is clean, partial+apply faults). Guard added, blob regen.
2. Batched o_proj/down_proj grids sized by _ceil_div(N, 64) -- the MSL tile width -- in BOTH
   branches, while the fallback branch dispatches the Mojo _pf_gemm_accum_kernel_i8 whose tiles
   are _GEMM_BN=32: only half the column tiles launched -> the second half of d_model never
   accumulated (per-layer hidden trace: down_proj contribution EXACTLY zero for columns 1024..2047
   of 2048). TinyLlama (d_ff=5632 % 384 != 0) is the first model on the down fallback. Grids are
   now kernel-family-conditional. (Any future model with n_q % 256 != 0 would have hit the same
   bug on o_proj.)

excuse; the delivered path IS the race. MEASURED (Qwen3-0.6B, raceA worker, one MojoRuntime,
consecutive decode() calls, 256-token prompt): call0 cold 3.2-3.8s ONE-TIME (worker start +
session first-use); same-shape warm calls 229-242ms for 64 tokens = 265-280 tok/s WALL
(worker-reported kernel rate 299-318). llama.cpp F16 same-session llama-bench tg64/tg256 = 240.8/
241.4. VERDICT: warm steady-state single-stream = WIN 1.11-1.16x; batched 2.1-3.2x stands.
THE TAX: switching request shape (max_new changes) pays a session rebuild -- probe sequence
64,64,256,64,256,256 gave wall rates 17(cold)/265/262/206/183/185 tok/s: the 256-shape calls
settle at ~1.39s = kernel ~815ms + prefill ~25ms + ~550ms rebuild; 64-after-256 pays ~70-140ms.

rebuild, not kernel). ADDRESS: mojo/engine/metaldispatch/qwen3_prefill_decode.mojo constructs a
FRESH _MBQwen3I8AllSimd7Prefill per request (5+ construction sites + upload_globals each); the
fix = persistent session across requests (open once; keep weights resident; per-shape KV
re-derivation only) -- parity-gap item 4 from 2026-08-09, now the TOP campaign priority because
it is the difference between "wins warm" and "wins unconditionally". The ~550ms breakdown
(upload/restore vs pipeline-build vs KV alloc) needs engine-side instrumentation before cutting.


## FIRST NVIDIA LLM INFERENCE — the CUDA-native resident session: Qwen3-0.6B on T4/L4/A100, oracle-exact, portable max.gpu.host only (2026-08-20)

Everything in this entry is the first of its kind in this tree: residentk kernels compiled for an
NVIDIA target, executed on real NVIDIA hardware, generating real Qwen3-0.6B-Base tokens — through
the PORTABLE `max.gpu.host` API (`DeviceContext` + checked `enqueue_function[kernel]`), with no
Metal shim and no metallib blobs anywhere in the path. The work landed on `feat/cuda-native-session`
(PR #778) in three phases; each phase's evidence is stated below, nothing inferred.

WHAT WAS BUILT
--------------
1. residentk on Mojo 1.0.0 (Phase 0). The resident GPU lane predated the 1.0 migration (#755) and
   did not compile on the pinned toolchain — invisible because CI never reaches it (it is private).
   Kernel scalar parameters are now fixed-width DevicePassable (`<name>_i64: Int64`, widened back
   to Int once at entry; Int64 keeps the Metal shim's 64-bit descriptor ABI byte-identical), and
   launches use 1.0.0's checked parameter form. Same dispatch plan, same numerics.
2. residentk.session_cuda._CudaResidentQwen3 (Phase 1): the CUDA-native session — resident f32
   weights, in-place KV cache, batched m_rows>1 PREFILL (new f32 tiled-GEMM twins of the `_pf_*`
   family in residentk/kernels_prefill_f32.mojo; the weightless batched kernels reused
   byte-unmodified), 128-row chunks, one lm_head+argmax on the final row; then the six-per-layer
   decode path per token, per-dispatch enqueue, NO batching/graphs yet. Gated behind
   `-D ALGENTA_GPU -D ALGENTA_CUDA` (the PR #765 two-tier split's first consumer on the resident
   path); a Metal or CPU build elides every launch.
3. Benchmarks (this section): benchmarks/llm_smoke/qwen3_generate_cuda.mojo (oracle driver) and
   qwen3_bench_cuda.mojo (benchmark driver).

ORACLE (Phase 2): exact
-------------------------
256-token race prompt ("The capital of France is Paris. " x36 + "The capital of France"), greedy,
weights converted on-VM from the Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base BF16 safetensors via the repo's own
`prepare_model_checkpoint()` (numpy, no torch). All three GPUs generated the campaign's exact
known-correct continuation — first 8 tokens [374, 12095, 13, 576, 6722, 315, 9625, 374], then the
7-token repeat cycle — 16/16 tokens checked per GPU, driver exits nonzero on any mismatch:

  Tesla T4  (sm_75, driver 595.71.05): RESULT: PASS — 16 greedy tokens match the campaign oracle
  NVIDIA L4 (sm_89, driver 595.71.05): RESULT: PASS — 16 greedy tokens match the campaign oracle
  A100-40GB (sm_80, driver 595.71.05): RESULT: PASS — 16 greedy tokens match the campaign oracle

Additionally, the FULL golden-vector suite (mojo/tests/libs/test_residentk_session.mojo — all five
resident arms against the frozen Float64 CPU reference) passed 51/51 on the T4 in Phase 0, and
still passes 51/51 on Apple M4 Max Metal at the branch HEAD — the Metal lane is preserved.

BENCHMARKS (Phase 3): first NVIDIA LLM numbers
----------------------------------------------
Methodology (stated, repeatable): ONE resident session per GPU; weights loaded once (untimed);
one full untimed WARMUP generation; then THREE timed generations of the same 256-token race
prompt replayed on the same session (every KV slot a replay reads is rewritten before it is read,
so replays are self-consistent); medians of the three. Timed scopes: PREFILL = the chunked batched
pass INCLUDING the lm_head+argmax that yields the first token; DECODE = the gen steps after
prefill, one per-dispatch-enqueue token each. Checkpoint: BF16 safetensors -> Float64 blob ->
resident Float32. Clock evidence: nvidia-smi 500 ms samplers ran alongside every timed window
(T4 boosted 300 -> 1590 MHz max under load; L4 held 2040 MHz max; A100 row below).

  GPU          | prefill tok/s (256 prompt) | decode tok/s gen=64 | decode tok/s gen=256
  -------------|----------------------------|---------------------|----------------------
  Tesla T4     | 120.9 (2117 ms)            | 51.6 (1241 ms)      | 43.9 (5829 ms)
  NVIDIA L4    | 274.8 (931 ms)             | 53.8 (1189 ms)      | 46.6 (5492 ms)
  A100-40GB    | 479.4 (534 ms)             | 70.1 (913 ms)       | 55.2 (4638 ms)

Per-run variance is small (T4 decode gen=64: 1238.1/1241.4/1242.2 ms; L4: 1188.5/1189.3/1188.9 ms)
— the medians are stable numbers, not lucky draws.

HONEST SCOPE — what these numbers are and are not
-------------------------------------------------
* They are FLOAT32-weight, per-dispatch-enqueue numbers: no CUDA graphs, no kernel fusion beyond
  the resident family's own, no quantization. The int8 Metal race arms are a different (faster)
  weight format; a CUDA int8 arm is future work, not claimed here.
* DECODE is dispatch-bound, not compute-bound: prefill scales 2.3x from T4 to L4 (bandwidth +
  compute both help the tiled GEMMs), but decode barely moves (51.6 -> 53.8). At 171 dispatches
  per token, the per-launch host cost is the dominant term — exactly the regime the Metal batched
  shim exists to delete on Metal, and exactly what a CUDA-graph capture/replay follow-up attacks
  on NVIDIA (see PR #778's integration notes). The bandwidth floor for f32 0.6B decode on a T4
  (~300 GB/s practical, 2.62 GB resident) is ~8-9 ms/token; the measured ~19 ms/token is mostly
  submission, not arithmetic.
* PREFILL tok/s here is the chunked batched path's first measurement; it is NOT raced against
  llama.cpp in this entry — the NVIDIA race front opens once the dispatch-bound decode is unbound.

COST LEDGER (spot, eplanev2)
----------------------------
Phase-0 T4 (n1-standard-4, ~15 min), Phase-2 first attempt (n1-standard-4, ~8 min, OOM'd the
conversion at 15 GB — the converter holds the whole Float64 tensor set in memory, so it needs a
~30 GB host; noted for the record), Phase-2/3 T4 (n1-standard-8, ~40 min), L4 first attempt
(g2-standard-4, ~12 min, same conversion OOM), L4 (g2-standard-8, ~20 min), A100
(a2-highgpu-1g, ~25 min). Total ~$2.50 spot. Every VM was deleted immediately after its suite;
no GPU idled unattended.

## LEVER 3a VERIFIED ON THE A100 — CUDA-graph decode arm oracle-exact, and the dispatch-bound diagnosis CORRECTED by measurement: host submission was NOT the binding constraint; the f32 kernel floors are, and the kernel-by-kernel sweep names them (2026-08-20)

The CUDA-graph decode arm (feat/nvidia-race-campaign, MAX 26.5's max.gpu.host.device_graph)
is built, and the oracle gate passed BEFORE any number counted — 16/16 greedy tokens match the
campaign continuation, verified twice: once with per-token host-fed state, and once as a single
async chain (the whole 15-token tail from back-to-back replays with a device-side token chain
and ONE synchronize). Both designs are in the tree; the bench races the async chain.

WHAT THE BUILD PAID FOR THE RECORD (integrity notes; each is documented where it lives)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
* Recorded host->device memcpy nodes read a CAPTURE-TIME SNAPSHOT of the host buffer, never
  live contents, and recorded device->host copies land in graph-owned staging, never the
  caller's buffer — bit-identical logits on every replay was the symptom. state_probe.mojo
  (benchmarks/llm_smoke/nvidia_race/) isolates all three facts. Fix: kernels-only capture,
  eager copies around the replay.
* Branded buffer origins convert to the kernels' mutable MutAnyOrigin parameters only at the
  enqueue call site, and an {imm} capture cannot take mutable pointers from self — the capture
  hoists Int(ptr) addresses and rebuilds the pointers via unsafe_from_address inside the build
  callback.
* The device-side generation chain (_graph_advance_kernel, captured last in the graph) logs
  each token to token_log[pos], feeds it as the next embed input, and advances pos/n_keys —
  N back-to-back replays run a whole generation with zero per-token host traffic.

THE NUMBERS (A100-SXM4-40GB, 20 runs/cell, frozen discipline)
--------------------------------------------------------------
  Arm                          prefill tok/s (256)     decode gen=64          verdicts
  per-dispatch (baseline)      483.0  (IQR 0.073%)     71.0  (IQR 0.019%)     PASS/PASS
  CUDA-graph async chain       482.7  (IQR 0.021%)     72.1  (IQR 0.007%)     PASS/PASS

THE DIAGNOSIS CORRECTION — stated plainly, because the ledger exists to do exactly this
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PR #778 named decode DISPATCH-BOUND (171 dispatches/token, decode flat across T4->L4->A100
while prefill scales). The graph arm tests that hypothesis directly: it deletes 170 of the 171
per-token enqueues (one replay, host-side cost near zero). Decode moves 71.0 -> 72.1 tok/s =
+1.6%, inside the noise band. HOST SUBMISSION WAS NOT THE BINDING CONSTRAINT on this stack —
the device-side kernel work itself is ~13.9 ms/token. The flat-across-GPUs signature that
motivated the original diagnosis has a second explanation the data cannot distinguish without
this experiment: kernels that run far below every GPU's floor on all three GPUs. The sweep
below shows that is the case.

KERNEL-BY-KERNEL SWEEP (kernel_sweep_cuda.mojo, same tree/GPU; REPS dispatches back-to-back,
one synchronize after the loop = device-bound windows; layer-0 shapes, real resident f32
weights; floors: A100-SXM4 HBM 1555 GB/s, FP32 SIMT 19.5 TFLOP/s — tensor cores not used by
these kernels; verdict bands frozen in the driver docstring)

  norm_gemv(qkv)        12.4 us  1350 GB/s   (87%)   ok            <- AT the bandwidth floor
  qk_rope_write          4.5 us    —                  dispatch-floor
  sdpa n_keys=256      233.3 us    9 GB/s   (0.6%)   very-low-bw   <- 136x BELOW the floor
  sdpa n_keys=512      461.6 us    9 GB/s   (0.6%)   very-low-bw   (linear in n_keys)
  sdpa n_keys=1024     920.3 us    9 GB/s   (0.6%)   very-low-bw

  pf_rmsnorm_rows         20 us    52 GB/s  (3.4%)   very-low-bw

VERDICTS AND THE OPTIMIZATION PLAN (measured-lever order, stated before the fixes are built)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. sdpa decode attention is the single largest decode cost: ~233 us x 28 layers = 6.5 ms of
   the ~13.9 ms token (47%), at 0.6% of the bandwidth floor — the barrier-tree reduction
   (9 barriers per key at d_head=128) is the mechanism. Metal solved exactly this with the
   warp-shuffle twin `_sdpa_kernel_simd` (2 barriers per key) — it is portable code, but its
   own docstring records a real codegen bug found on Metal/1.0.0b2 (lane-0/1 zero-contribution,
   ~1% of dispatches at production shapes), so it gets a dedicated NVIDIA correctness probe
   BEFORE adoption, not a blind dispatch swap. Expected if clean: ~5.5-6 ms/token back.
2. Prefill's tiled GEMMs run at 1.7-3.0% of the FP32 SIMT peak — naive tiling, no vectorized
   loads, no double-buffering. llama.cpp's 14.3k tok/s warm pp256 rides FP16 tensor cores;
   SIMT f32 cannot get there. The honest levers, in order: (a) vectorized/buffered tiling for
   a few x, (b) an f16-activation/f16-weight GEMM path if the toolchain exposes tensor-core
   mma on NVIDIA, (c) otherwise prefill is documented as the format/architecture gap rather
   than tuned away.
3. Weight format: the GEMV family already runs at 54-102% of HBM peak in f32 — the only way
   to move them is fewer BYTES: the f16 CUDA session (Phase 3b; the Metal f16 family exists
   and is portable) halves every GEMV + the lm_head stream; int8 halves again. This is also
   the format-fair race arm (F16 vs llama.cpp F16).
4. Dispatch/launch floor: embed/ropewrt/argmax_reduce sit at 3.8-5.4 us each — the graph arm
   already deletes their submission cost; nothing left there.

WHAT CLOSED THE GAP, MECHANISM BY MECHANISM
--------------------------------------------
* CUDA-graph arm (session_cuda.step_graph / seed_and_run_graph): one captured graph per
  session, a device-side generation chain (_graph_advance_kernel: logs the token, feeds it as
  the next embed input, advances pos/n_keys) so N back-to-back replays run a whole generation
  with ZERO per-token host traffic. Kernels-only capture — state_probe.mojo proved recorded
  memcpy nodes (both directions) never touch the caller's buffers; the feed and readback are
  eager copies around the replay. The +1.6% over per-dispatch is the honest measurement that
  host submission was NOT the bottleneck on this stack — the kernels were.
* Warp-shuffle attention reduction: sdpa ran at 0.6% of the bandwidth floor (9 barriers/key);
  the simd-shuffle twin cut that to 2 (1.38x standalone). Its docstring documents a real
  codegen bug on Metal/1.0.0b2 — sdpa_simd_nvidia_probe.mojo re-ran the exact minimal repro
  (d_head=32/n_keys=1, 100% deterministic there) x100 plus 2000-dispatch production stress on
  the A100: 0 mismatches, worst diff 3e-7 — the bug does not exist on NVIDIA/mojo 1.0.0.
* Split-K flash-decoding in the capture: 16 blocks (one per head) on 108 SMs was the sweep's
  named occupancy wall; N_SPLITS fan-out recruits h_q x N_SPLITS blocks. Inside a captured
  graph the extra dispatch costs nothing, so the Metal-side ~500-key crossover (a launch-
  overhead argument) does not apply — the sweep 8/16/32/64 = 262.9/307.1/329.8/328.0 shows
  the plateau at 32.

THE WEIGHT-FORMAT ARMS — MEASURED, DIAGNOSED, TOOLCHAIN-BLOCKED (stated plainly)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The F16 CUDA session was BUILT and oracle-verified 16/16 (session_cuda_f16: f16 weights via
the Metal-proven _f16 kernel twins, f16 prefill GEMM twins in kernels_prefill_f16, same graph
decode arm). It measured 87.1/84.2 tok/s decode — 3x SLOWER than f32, the opposite of halved
bytes. The probe battery (benchmarks/llm_smoke/nvidia_race/) isolated why, each probe a
committed artifact:
  * f16_gemv_probe: the f16 GEMV family runs at 5.5-6.9% of HBM peak on NVIDIA (86-108 GB/s)
    vs 53-91% for the f32 twins.
  * f16_vec8_probe: width-8 f16 loads are WORSE (23-62 GB/s) — vector width is not the
    variable.
  * f16_stream_probe: the f16->f32 cast costs ~2x, but Int32 loads of the SAME bytes are just
    as slow — it is the load path, not the cast.
  * i8_gemv_probe: the int8 family (char4 loads, the Metal race arm's kernels) collapses to
    1.0-1.6% of peak.
  * i8_via_int32_probe: even Int32-typed SIMD loads run at ~2% of peak in the GEMV shape.
  VERDICT: in the Mojo 1.0.0 / MAX 26.5 CUDA backend, ONLY Float32 vector loads stream at HBM
  speed; every sub-f32 SIMD load path is scalarized. MAX exposes TMA but no tensor-core mma
  surface to route around it, and the toolchain has no value-level bit-reinterpretation
  primitive to unpack f16/i8 bytes loaded as f32 words. The quantized/f16 arms are therefore
  toolchain-blocked, not kernel-blocked; the f16 session stays in-tree (correct, race-ready)
  for the day the backend load paths are fixed, and the race rows stand on f32 until then.

WHAT REMAINS BETWEEN HERE AND A WIN — costed honestly
------------------------------------------------------
* Decode (0.92x): the residual ~1.5 ms/token is dominated by the f32 weight streams already at
  54-91% of HBM peak plus the 616 MB f32 lm_head stream (446 us at 90% of peak). Inside f32
  there is nothing left to take; the win requires either the backend f16/i8 load fix or a
  tensor-core surface — both upstream of this repo.
* Prefill (482.6 tok/s vs llama-bench warm 14330 F16): the tiled GEMMs run at 1.7-3.0% of FP32
  SIMT peak (kernel sweep above) — naive tiling, no double-buffering. The honest path is a
  register-blocked/double-buffered tiled GEMM (days of kernel work, 5-10x headroom measured in
  the gap to SIMT peak), then the same format question as decode. Recorded as the next
  campaign phase, not taken in this round.

WHAT LANDED — the v2 prefill GEMM family (residentk/kernels_prefill_f32_v2.mojo, wired into
residentk.session_cuda.prefill for all four roles)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Mechanism-by-mechanism against the first generation's measured losses (1.7-3.0% of the A100's
19.5 TFLOP/s FP32 SIMT peak):
* REGISTER BLOCK 4x4 on a 64x64 output tile, 256 threads: 16 accumulator scalars per thread
  (declared as 16 explicit `var`s — registers by construction), 16 FMAs per k-step against 8
  shared loads = a 2:1 FMA:LDS mix vs the first generation's 1:1 (2x2 block, 4 FMAs / 4 loads).
* SOFTWARE PIPELINING: two shared copies of each tile; the next tile's float4 loads are in
  flight while the current tile is consumed. ONE barrier per k-step serves both directions,
  where the first generation used two barriers per step and hid no latency.
* VECTORIZED GLOBAL LOADS: exactly one `load[width=4]` (128-bit float4) per thread per tile —
  the proven surface (the probe battery: Float32 vector loads are the ONLY SIMD loads that
  stream at HBM speed on this backend, so v2 stays inside it).
* BANK-CONFLICT-AWARE SHARED LAYOUTS: A row stride BK+4 (moves the 4-row register-block read
  stride off one bank set); B stored TRANSPOSED [BK][BN+1] with column ownership c = tx+16*j
  (conflict-free inner-loop reads; ~2-way scatter-writes, accepted and measured, not argued).

THE SIMT-F32 ARITHMETIC CEILING, MEASURED (f16_simd_arith_probe.mojo, new this round)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The question the optimization plan needed answered before declaring headroom spent: what does
this backend actually deliver for FP32 SIMD arithmetic? Answer, measured with a compute-bound
FMA-chain probe (no loads in the timed loop, 432 blocks x 256 threads, 4096 iterations):
  f32 SIMD[4]:  17.6 TFLOP/s = 90% of the nominal 19.5 TFLOP/s FP32 SIMT peak
  f16 SIMD[8]:  60.5 TFLOP/s (~3.4x the f32 rate — packed f16x2 FMAs DO lower)
INTEGRITY — the probe only counts after three catches, each documented in its source:
  (1) RECURRENCE-DOUBLING: Mojo lowers FP with reassociation enabled, so any LINEAR FMA
      recurrence a' = a*b + c gets folded by LLVM from 4096 iterations to ~20 FMAs — with a
      CONSTANT coefficient AND with a runtime one. First two probe versions reported 300-457%
      of the physical peak; the embedded PTX proved the fold. The shipped probe uses a coupled
      NONLINEAR recurrence (each accumulator multiplies its neighbour), which cannot fold.
  (2) DEAD LANES: a `sink[0]` store lets DCE kill SIMD lanes 1-3 — ncu's executed-FFMA counter
      showed exactly 1/4 of the claimed work running. The shipped probe stores all lanes' sum.
  (3) HARDWARE WITNESS: ncu (cuda-nsight-compute) counted 7,248,199,680 executed thread-FFMAs
      vs 7,247,757,312 expected (0.006% — the delta is seed/epilogue FMAs). The timing is now
      witness-verified, not just plausible.
VERDICT: the v2 GEMMs at 12-38% of peak are NOT at the arithmetic ceiling (90% measured) —
the remainder is shared-memory traffic, grid fill on the narrow-N roles, and the HBM feed;
further SIMT-f32 gains are possible but diminishing, and none of them change the headline
result or close the warm-vs-warm tensor-core gap below.

THE TENSOR-CORE BATTERY, RE-CONFIRMED DEFINITIVE (mma_surface_probe.sh + this round's runtime
evidence — task item 3's "re-confirm for mma", done)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
* 15 compile probes on the pinned Mojo 1.0.0 / MAX 26.5 toolchain, sm_80 target: NO
  std.gpu.mma / std.gpu.primitives.mma / max.gpu.mma / max.gpu.tensor_core / std.tensor_core
  module, NO tma module at those paths, NO mma/mma_sync name inside max.gpu / std.gpu /
  max.gpu.host, NO inline-asm escape hatch (std.sys.inline_asm absent, __builtin_asm unknown).
* The internal `_cublas` / `_cudnn` modules EXIST (they import) but expose no callable
  sgemm/gemm/math-mode surface under 45+ probed names (C API spellings, snake_case, Mojo
  idioms) — they are MAX Engine's JIT-internal bindings, not a user surface; `matmul_rs`
  fails to link ('linalg' absent) on this install.
* RUNTIME refinement of the f16 question (new): f16 SIMD ARITHMETIC executes packed and fast
  (60.5 TF/s above), but the campaign's probe battery already measured every sub-f32 LOAD
  path scalarized (5-7% of HBM peak) — so the f16 arithmetic rate cannot be fed by f16
  weights at HBM speed, and an f16-accumulation GEMM would also break the exact-token oracle.
  Recorded as a NAMED FUTURE LEVER (ready-made for both GEMM and GEMV the day the backend
  load paths are fixed), NOT an adopted arm.
CONCLUSION, stated plainly: no tensor-core surface is routeable from Mojo user code on this
toolchain; the warm-vs-warm prefill gap to llama.cpp (0.23x of 14101 tok/s) and the decode
format gap (0.92x/0.87x) are BOTH the weight-format / tensor-core gap, upstream of this repo.
That is the definitive, measured ceiling the campaign stops at.

PROVISIONING GOTCHA (new this round, fixed in-line, recorded for the next VM)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
On the 22.04 GCP image, `ubuntu-drivers install --gpgpu` now pulls the 595.84 NON-server
stack; installing the matching prebuilt kernel module then conflict-REMOVES the userspace,
leaving nvidia-smi absent after the reboot. Fix (run on this VM): `sudo apt-get install -y
nvidia-utils-595-server libnvidia-compute-595-server`, then reboot — the -server userspace
coexists with the -server kernel module (595.71.05, same series as the first A100 round).
setup_vm.sh's stage-2 broadened detection covered the package-set discovery; this conflict
ordering is the a2-specific variant of the g2/L4 gotcha its 2026-08-21 hardening documented.
ALSO: port 22 to this VM was filtered from the build host — every ssh/scp ran through
`--tunnel-through-iap` (slower but reliable); the VM needed `--network=default
--subnet=default` (custom-subnet-mode project) and the older gcloud's `--preemptible`.

Pre-fix smoke C=8 was 33/40 on BOTH GPUs — the stdin bug below. Post-fix: every subsequent
matrix cell 64/64.

FIX 1 — qwen3_serve_cuda.mojo stdin reader (THE RACE-CRITICAL FIX; port to a repo PR).
Root cause (measured on both VMs): Mojo 1.0.0 `input()` drops every buffered byte past the
FIRST newline of each internal refill. Repro: two 4246-byte JSON request lines in ONE pipe
write → input() returns line 1, then a 302-byte tail fragment, and loses the ~3.9KB middle.
Three short lines in one write → only line 1 survives. At harness concurrency ≥8 several
lines are always in flight in the stdin pipe, so input() silently loses requests, the driver
idles in pipe_read, and the harness errors the orphans at its 600s deadline (observed: smoke
C=8 ok=33/40 on BOTH GPUs; phase-1 C=8 cell same). Attempted fix v1 used
FileHandle.read_bytes(4096) on /dev/stdin — it DEADLOCKS: read_bytes(n) waits for the full n
bytes or EOF and stalls on a partial line's tail. Fix v2 (landed): read ONE byte per
read_bytes(1) call (a 1-byte read(2) returns as soon as any byte arrives — nothing dropped,
nothing stalls). Verbatim diff preserved as serve_stdin_fix.diff (54 lines; adds struct
_StdinLines + swaps input() → stdin_lines.next_line() in _serve_loop). Validated:
split-write + two-lines-one-write protocol tests PASS; smoke C=8 40/40; all phase-1 cells
64/64.

FIX 2 — build syntax for Mojo 1.0.0: struct methods must use `def` (`fn` was removed).

No other compile fixes: packed3 probe and serve driver both built PLAIN (no object+link
fallback needed) on sm_80 and sm_89.
